newsitem.title: USA: SEC's Levitt mum on solid waste bond probe-letter.
newsitem.headline: SEC's Levitt mum on solid waste bond probe-letter.

text.p: SEC chairman Arthur Levitt told a key U.S. senator that he cannot disclose whether the agency is reviewing concerns about muni bonds issued to finance solid waste facilities, according to a one-page letter released Tuesday.

But the aide to Sen. Bob Smith, who chairs the Senate's subcommittee on waste control, said a Securities and Exchange Commission staff member told him in a telephone conversation that SEC is in fact looking into the matter.
Smith, R-N.H., asked Levitt in April to examine whether localities that issued bonds to build solid waste disposal sites in recent years adequately disclosed investment risks to investors.

Were investors told of flow control's uncertain legal status in the wake of a key 1994 U.S. Supreme Court ruling on the issue, Smith asked for instance. And did investment documents discuss potential for default, he asked.
In addition, Rep. Bill Pascrell, D-N.J., told Smith's panel March 18 that some New Jersey counties have bonded for facilities that were never built.
Levitt told Smith, "I have relayed the concerns raised in your correspondence to our Division of Enforcement."

"The Commission staff carefully evaluates complaints concerning possible violations of the federal securities laws. Unfortunately, I cannot inform you of what enforcement inquiries have been or will be made" because of confidentiality concerns, Levitt said.

Levitt noted that unlike corporate securities, municipal bonds are not subject to registration and reporting provisions of the securities laws. They are, however, subject to the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, he said.
Flow control refers to the ability of local governments to require that municipal solid waste generated within a jurisdiction be processed at a designated disposal site.
